items.title: Emotional valence experiences, not sensory valence: Clarifying James’s theory of emotion: Reply to Roelofs (2026).
items.content: Roelofs (2026) argues that our findings, showing that pleasant and unpleasant feelings follow Weber’s law, do not support William James’s theory of emotion because James excluded such feelings from his account. We address this claim by offering two clarifications. First, we argue that this conclusion rests on a mismatch between James’s terminology and the terms as used in contemporary affective science. While James excluded (un)pleasant feelings from his theory, he excluded basic (un)pleasant affective qualities perceived as inherent properties of the stimulus itself, what he termed “tone of feeling,” but he did not exclude valence experiences. What distinguishes between the two levels are the objects, for example, “this picture is ugly” (tone of feeling) versus “this picture makes me feel unpleasant” (valence experiences). In our experiments, participants reported about their (un)pleasant emotional state. This corresponds to what James conceptualized as a “felt state of excitement,” an intense subjective state attributed to the experiencer that he explicitly identified as the defining feature of emotion rather than excluding it. Second, we clarify that our reference to James was intended to situate our findings within the broader historical tradition of perceptual theories of emotion rather than to support the specific details of his original account. Ultimately, once the terminology is aligned, it becomes clear that our results are entirely consistent with James’s framework. In fact, they provide modern empirical support for his core vision: that emotions are, at their essence, perceptual processes. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Weber’s law in feelings does not support James’s theory of emotions: Commentary on Berkovich and Meiran (2023, 2024).
items.content: Using an evidence-accumulation model of feeling generation to analyze manual responses, Berkovich and Meiran (2023, 2024) observed that feelings of pleasure and displeasure evoked by stimuli follow Weber’s law (Weber, 1834, 1846). They regarded this finding as strong support, and perhaps the strongest yet, for James’s (1884) theory of emotions, according to which emotions are sensory experiences of bodily changes. Here, I argue that Weber’s law in feelings cannot, strictly speaking, support James’s sensory theory, simply because he excluded feelings of pleasure and displeasure from his theory. James (1894) made this particularly clear in response to Lehmann (1892), who observed that the bodily change (i.e., change in heartbeat and respiration) evoked by stimuli developed after the feeling of pleasure or displeasure was reported, and that therefore the experience of the change could not be the feeling. In modern physiological studies, central indicators of pleasure and displeasure have also been found to precede peripheral bodily changes. Furthermore, the primary interoceptive and proprioceptive brain areas were not found to be activated during pleasure and displeasure, compared to a neutral state. So even if we were to extend James’s theory to feelings of pleasure and displeasure, Berkovich and Meiran’s findings, in the absence of physiological evidence to the contrary, would not support the theory.
